confirmed.title: Zero infohash from untrusted BEP-46 pointer panics the daemon
confirmed.description: AddInfoHash calls e.client.AddTorrentInfoHash(metainfo.Hash(infoHash)) with no zero-infohash guard and no recover(). anacrolix's AddTorrentInfoHashWithStorage (client.go:~1514) executes panicif.Zero(infoHash). FetchCompanionTorrent -> AddInfoHash is reached with an infohash taken from companion.Subscriber, which sources it from AnacrolixGetter.GetInfohashPointer (dht.go:211). GetInfohashPointerInfo validates only len(v.IH)==20, not non-zero, so a malicious publisher can publish a BEP-46 content-index pointer whose IH field is 20 zero bytes. That returns [20]byte{} all the way into AddInfoHash, panicif.Zero fires, the panic propagates up the companion subscriber goroutine (no recover anywhere in subscriber.go or the daemon goroutine at subscriber.go:446), and the daemon crashes. Unlike AddMagnetURI, AddInfoHash has no defensive recover. This is a remote, unauthenticated DoS.
confirmed.suggestion: In AddInfoHash, reject a zero infohash before calling the client: `if (infoHash == [20]byte{}) { return nil, errors.New("engine: zero infohash") }`. Ideally also add the same non-zero check in dhtindex.GetInfohashPointerInfo (fail closed at the parse boundary) so every consumer is protected, and/or wrap AddInfoHash's client call in a recover() mirroring AddMagnetURI.

confirmed.title: autoDownload flips a restored paused torrent's files to Normal priority
confirmed.description: registerLocked unconditionally spawns autoDownload(h). restoreEntry only sets h.paused and calls DisallowDataDownload/Upload AFTER registerLocked returns. autoDownload waits on GotInfo, but for a file-restored torrent GotInfo is already closed, so autoDownload can proceed to queueOrActivate -> activateDownload and flip every file to PiecePriorityNormal concurrently with (or before) restoreEntry's DisallowDataDownload call. Neither queueOrActivate nor activateDownload consult h.IsPaused(). Result: a torrent the user explicitly paused last session has its piece priorities set to Normal on restore, and there is a race window where anacrolix may begin requesting pieces before DisallowDataDownload lands. Even after Disallow wins, File.Priority reads back as 'normal' on a paused torrent, which is inconsistent state.
confirmed.suggestion: Make activateDownload (or queueOrActivate) skip when h.IsPaused() is true, and/or set the paused state + Disallow in restoreEntry before registerLocked spawns the goroutines (e.g. apply paused state inside the locked section or pass an initial-paused flag into registerLocked). On Resume, re-run activateDownload to flip priorities back on.

confirmed.title: Inbound LTEP message handler spawns an unbounded goroutine per frame before rate-limiting applies
confirmed.description: PeerConnReadExtensionMessage spawns a fresh goroutine (plus copies the payload) for every sn_search-tagged frame, and HandleMessage spawns yet another goroutine per reply. The swarmsearch per-peer rate limiter only drops work *inside* HandleMessage, after the goroutine and payload copy already exist. A peer that floods sn_search frames forces one goroutine + one payload allocation per frame regardless of the limiter. While each goroutine is short-lived once the limiter drops the message, a high-rate flood still imposes unbounded transient goroutine/alloc churn driven entirely by remote input, with no admission control at the spawn site. The reply path spawning a second goroutine per write compounds this if a peer can keep many queries pending.
confirmed.suggestion: Gate the spawn with a bounded worker pool or a buffered semaphore (e.g. a per-engine `chan struct{}` of fixed capacity; drop-and-log when full), so inbound frame volume can't translate into unbounded goroutine creation before the protocol-layer limiter is consulted. Consider checking the per-peer limiter (cheaply) before spawning.

confirmed.title: Restored paused torrent never reaches the queue/promotion accounting consistently
confirmed.description: On restore, queueOrder is reapplied and upgradeMagnetSession/verifyOnRestore are spawned, but queueOrActivate is only reached via the autoDownload goroutine, which ignores the cap-vs-paused interaction (see the paused-priority finding). Combined with countActiveDownloads counting metadata-only torrents as active, a batch restore of many torrents can momentarily exceed maxActiveDownloads before queue accounting settles, since each handle's autoDownload independently calls queueOrActivate and reads countActiveDownloads without a global serialization point. Impact is transient over-subscription, not corruption.
confirmed.suggestion: Consider promoting/queueing restored torrents through a single serialized pass after RestoreSession finishes adding all entries, rather than relying on N independent autoDownload goroutines racing on countActiveDownloads.

confirmed.title: autoConfirmOnComplete leaks a goroutine for up to 24h after RemoveTorrent
confirmed.description: autoConfirmOnComplete selects on h.T.Complete().On() or a 24h timer, but does not select on e.bgCtx.Done(). If a torrent is removed (RemoveTorrent drops it) or the engine context is cancelled before completion, this goroutine lingers until the torrent completes or the 24h timer fires. Close() doesn't wait on or cancel it. Low impact (bounded by 24h and one per torrent) but inconsistent with the bgCtx-aware pattern used by verifyOnRestore and the prune goroutine.
confirmed.suggestion: Add `case <-e.bgCtx.Done(): return` to the select so removal/shutdown reclaims the goroutine promptly.

confirmed.title: AllTorrentDocs silently drops the SignedBy field on reconstruction
confirmed.description: AllTorrentDocs projects fieldInfoHash, fieldName, fieldFilePaths, fieldTrackers, fieldSizeBytes, fieldFileCount, fieldAddedAt but NOT fieldSignedBy, and torrentDocFromFields never reads SignedBy. The schema-v3 bump exists specifically to carry the signer pubkey (identity/load-bearing per the architecture), yet a TorrentDoc round-tripped through AllTorrentDocs always comes back with SignedBy="". Today the only caller (companion BuildFromIndex) doesn't read SignedBy so no live data loss, but the method documents itself as reconstructing torrent docs 'from the stored fields' — the next caller that needs publisher attribution (e.g. a companion index that wants to record who signed each torrent) will silently get empty signers and have no error to detect it. Concrete failure: add a publisher-attribution feature to companion build, populate TorrentRecord.SignedBy from AllTorrentDocs, and every record ships unsigned despite the index holding the pubkey.
confirmed.suggestion: Add fieldSignedBy to the sr.Fields projection in AllTorrentDocs and add a SignedBy reconstruction line (`if v, ok := fields[fieldSignedBy].(string); ok { doc.SignedBy = v }`) to torrentDocFromFields, mirroring how Search() already projects and reads it. Add a test that indexes a signed torrent and asserts AllTorrentDocs returns the SignedBy.

confirmed.title: Stats CorpusTextBytes silently undercounts above 64,000 content docs
confirmed.description: The content-text scan loop is bounded by `guardTTL = 64` over a batch of 1000, so it sums at most 64,000 content docs. ContentCount (read from res.Total) is accurate, but CorpusTextBytes and the derived InflationRatio stop accumulating past 64k docs with no error and no warning. Since content docs are one-per-file-chunk and large files are chunked at ~10KB, a single large text-heavy torrent (or a busy node) can exceed 64k chunks, after which the reported corpus size and inflation ratio are wrong and there is no signal that they're truncated. This directly defeats the documented purpose of the metric ('how big is Bleve's index per TB of indexed text'). The TorrentCount/ContentCount counts loop is fine (Size=0, reads Total); only the text-sum loop is capped.
confirmed.suggestion: Either remove the fixed guardTTL and terminate purely on `len(res.Hits) < batch` (the from += batch advancement already guarantees forward progress and termination), or scale the guard off ContentCount (e.g. guardTTL = ContentCount/batch + 2), and/or log a warning when the guard is hit so a truncated metric is observable rather than silent.

confirmed.title: infohash interpolated into Bleve QueryString without escaping
confirmed.description: ContentDocsForInfoHash and DeleteContentForTorrent build a Bleve QueryString by string-concatenating the infohash (`+infohash:<value>`). QueryString syntax has reserved characters (+ - : ^ ~ " * ? whitespace) that would change query semantics. This is safe today only because every HTTP caller validates infohash as exactly 40 hex chars before reaching the engine, and hex has no reserved chars. But the indexer itself performs no validation, so a future internal caller passing an unvalidated or attacker-influenced infohash (e.g. from a parsed companion index or DHT payload) could cause a malformed query — at worst a query parse error (fail-closed: nothing deleted), at worst a query that matches/deletes the wrong docs. The Search SignedBy path already does the right thing using NewTermQuery + SetField instead of string interpolation.
confirmed.suggestion: Replace the QueryString interpolation in ContentDocsForInfoHash and DeleteContentForTorrent with a conjunction of NewTermQuery(typeContent).SetField(fieldType) and NewTermQuery(lower(infohash)).SetField(fieldInfoHash), matching the structured-query approach already used for the SignedBy filter in Search. This removes the escaping concern entirely and keeps keyword-field matching exact.

confirmed.title: deleteByQueryLocked has no terminal bound if a delete is silently ineffective
confirmed.description: deleteByQueryLocked loops re-querying from offset 0 and relies on each Batch delete shrinking the result set to terminate (it returns when a partial batch is seen or zero hits). This is correct for synchronous Bleve scorch deletes. However, unlike Stats/AllTorrentDocs there is no defensive iteration guard, so if a delete ever fails to remove a matching doc while the Batch call still returns success (e.g. an ID Search returns but Delete is a no-op for that doc), the loop would spin forever holding i.mu, deadlocking every other index operation. Low probability given current Bleve semantics, but worth a cheap guard given the global-mutex blast radius.
confirmed.suggestion: Add a bounded iteration guard (mirroring Stats's guardTTL pattern, scaled off the initial Total or a generous fixed ceiling) and return an error if the loop fails to make progress (deleted count unchanged across an iteration), so the path fails closed rather than hanging the index mutex.

confirmed.title: Subtitle extractor ignores maxBytes and has no size guard — unbounded memory on hostile .srt
confirmed.description: Extract() explicitly ignores its maxBytes parameter (comment at line 47-49) and wraps the raw reader in a bufio.Scanner with a 1 MiB per-line buffer, accumulating every dialog line into an unbounded strings.Builder. The pipeline relies on each extractor to apply the 100 MiB global cap via its own io.LimitReader (see pipeline.go safeExtract / engine.go NewPipeline(...,100*1024*1024)), but subtitle never does. The claims() init function also has no c.Size guard (unlike pdf/mkv/flac/etc.). A peer can ship a 2+ GiB file named episode.srt consisting entirely of valid cue text (no NUL bytes); it dispatches to SubtitleExtractor and is read fully into RAM, OOM-killing the daemon. This is a remotely-triggerable DoS via ordinary torrent content.
confirmed.suggestion: Wrap the reader in io.LimitReader(r, maxBytes) (defaulting maxBytes when <=0, as the other extractors do) before constructing the scanner, and add a `if c.Size > someCap { return false }` guard to the claims function. A subtitle file legitimately never exceeds a few MiB.

confirmed.title: MKV readFull(int(size)) allocates from an unbounded untrusted VINT size
confirmed.description: In Extract's segment-child loop, for Info/Tracks/Chapters/Tags elements the code calls readFull(br, int(size)) where size is a uint64 EBML VINT parsed directly from file bytes (parseVINT yields up to 2^56-1). readFull (flac.go:178-184) does make([]byte, n) BEFORE the io.ReadFull, so the allocation happens regardless of the 16 MiB LimitReader on the input. A crafted MKV whose Tracks element declares size=5_000_000_000 forces a 5 GB allocation; ReadFull then fails at EOF but the memory is already requested. For size>maxInt make panics (caught by recover), but for multi-GB sizes that fit int the process attempts the allocation and gets OOM-killed. Same readFull is reachable in ogg.go (segCount/total bounded to ~65 KB, so OK there) but mkv's size is unbounded.
confirmed.suggestion: Bound size before allocating: reject or clamp when size exceeds maxBytes (or a small metadata cap, e.g. a few MiB) before calling readFull. e.g. `if size > uint64(maxBytes) { break }`. Better, have readFull itself refuse n beyond a sane ceiling.

confirmed.title: ZIP/XML/PDF extractors cap input but not decompressed output (zip-bomb amplification)
confirmed.line: 51-85 (and odt.go, odp.go, pptx.go, epub.go, pdf.go, htmltext.go)
confirmed.description: The global 100 MiB cap (engine.go) and each extractor's io.LimitReader bound only the *compressed* input buffer. Decompressed text is then accumulated into an unbounded strings.Builder: docx/odt/odp/pptx via the XML token decoder's `out`, epub via `combined` across all chapters, pdf via io.ReadAll(GetPlainText()), htmltext via `out`. archive/zip and the flate/FlateDecode streams have no decompression-ratio limit, so a ~100 MiB OOXML/PDF whose single content part is a highly compressible payload can expand to multiple GB of in-memory text before chunkText runs. Unlike the ZIM extractor (which enforces emitted>=maxBytes), none of these stop accumulating. Recover() does not help — OOM is not a recoverable panic. RTF is the counter-example done right: it breaks when out.Len() > maxBytes.
confirmed.suggestion: Add an output-size guard mirroring rtf.go: track builder length while decoding and stop (return partial text) once it exceeds maxBytes (or a dedicated text cap). For pdf, read GetPlainText() through io.LimitReader. This gives the same defense ZIM already has.

confirmed.title: ID3 pre-allocates up to 256 MiB from header tagSize independent of file size
confirmed.description: tagSize := syncSafeInt(header[6:10]) yields up to 2^28-1 (~256 MiB); the code then does raw := make([]byte, 10+tagSize) before io.ReadFull. A 20-byte .mp3 whose ID3 header claims tagSize=0xFFFFFFF forces a 256 MiB allocation per file; ReadFull then errors at EOF and the buffer is discarded. Bounded to 256 MiB so not catastrophic alone, but a torrent of many such tiny files processed concurrently multiplies it. The allocation is also wasteful because tagSize is not validated against the available input.
confirmed.suggestion: Clamp tagSize to min(tagSize, maxBytes) and/or to the remaining input length before make, or read incrementally. The actual frame loop already bounds itself by len(frames), so reading only what exists is safe.

confirmed.title: Extract watchdog is soft-only with no context cancellation — wedged extractor leaks a goroutine forever
confirmed.description: safeExtract arms a 60s timer that only logs pipeline.extract_slow; it cannot interrupt the extractor (the Extractor interface takes no context.Context, acknowledged in commit 2b96949). If an extractor enters a pathological loop or blocks on a slow/stalled torrent reader, the pipeline worker goroutine is stuck indefinitely with no terminal/failure transition — an ambiguous-limbo state that violates the 'bounded recovery / fail-closed' rule. The size cap is the only real protection, and as the findings above show it is not airtight (subtitle, mkv, decompressed output). One wedged file permanently consumes a worker; enough of them deadlock extraction throughput.
confirmed.suggestion: Plumb a context.Context into Extractor.Extract (or at minimum run Extract in a child goroutine selected against a hard deadline so the worker can move on and mark the file failed, accepting the leaked goroutine as the documented tradeoff). Pair with the output caps so genuinely-stuck cases are rare.

confirmed.title: Random (non-LRU) cluster cache eviction can thrash on cross-cluster article ordering
confirmed.description: clusterCache evicts half its entries by ranging the map (Go's non-deterministic map iteration order) when it hits cacheCap=32. The comment justifies this by assuming URL-pointer order is roughly cluster-sorted, but ZIM files are URL-sorted, not cluster-sorted, so adjacent articles frequently live in different clusters. Random eviction can drop a cluster that is about to be reused, re-triggering a zstd DecodeAll (up to 64 MiB) — a performance cliff on real Kiwix files, not a correctness bug. It also makes per-run cluster decode counts non-deterministic, though final output is deterministic.
confirmed.suggestion: If this shows up in profiling, switch to a small LRU (e.g. container/list-backed) keyed by ClusterNum. Otherwise document that eviction is best-effort and leave as-is.

confirmed.title: Responder sync sessions are unbounded and never reaped
confirmed.description: onSyncBegin registers a SyncSession keyed by (peerAddr, txid) and only releases it on the zero-record path or when a matching sync_end arrives. There is no per-peer session cap and no staleness/timeout reaper (confirmed: no reap/expire/CreatedAt logic anywhere in the package). A peer that advertised BitSetReconciliation can send thousands of sync_begin frames with distinct txids and non-empty matching filters; each call creates a session via NewSyncSession that snapshots the ENTIRE local record set into a map + RIBLT encoder + decoder, then leaves it registered indefinitely if the initiator never sends sync_end. This is unbounded memory growth with no terminal failure path - a determinism-violation (ambiguous limbo state) and a practical DoS.
confirmed.suggestion: Add a max-sessions-per-peer cap in registerSyncSession (reject/evict oldest beyond e.g. 4) and stamp each session with a creation time, then run a bounded reaper (or check on each frame) that releases sessions older than a stale threshold and emits sync_end aborted. Charge misbehavior when a peer exceeds the per-peer session cap.

confirmed.title: RIBLT decoder ignores the on-wire symbol Index, silently desyncing on a dropped frame
confirmed.description: SyncSymbols carries an Index field (first symbol's position) precisely so sender/receiver symbol positions stay aligned, but ApplySymbols never reads m.Index - it just calls dec.AddRemoteSymbol, which derives the position from its own running len(diffSymbols). The encoder side (onSyncBegin/ProduceSymbols) likewise advances its own counter. If any intermediate sync_symbols frame is dropped (e.g. a frame that fails DecodeSyncSymbols and is dropped in handleSyncFrame, or a future batched/heartbeat path), the encoder index and decoder index permanently desync and reconciliation produces wrong differences or never converges, with no error surfaced. The Index field gives a free integrity check that is currently unused.
confirmed.suggestion: In ApplySymbols, validate that m.Index equals the decoder's expected next index (s.symbolsIn) and abort the session with status aborted on mismatch, rather than blindly appending.

confirmed.title: ShareLocal==1 (swarm-only) leaks the full local index
confirmed.description: Capabilities.ShareLocal==1 is documented as 'answer queries only for torrents in the current swarm', but handleQuery only special-cases ShareLocal==0 (reject). For both 1 and 2 it calls searcher.SearchLocal over the entire Bleve index with no swarm-membership filter. An operator who sets ShareLocal=1 expecting to expose only currently-swarmed torrents instead exposes their whole index to every querying peer - a privacy/capability-correctness violation. DefaultCapabilities uses 2, so this only bites custom configs, but it silently does the opposite of the documented contract.
confirmed.suggestion: Either enforce swarm-membership filtering for ShareLocal==1 (requires a swarm-aware searcher), or, until that exists, document/treat ShareLocal==1 as unsupported and fail closed (reject) rather than serving the full index.

confirmed.title: StartFeeler claims idempotency but spawns a goroutine on every call
confirmed.description: The doc comment says 'Safe to call multiple times (subsequent calls are no-ops if a feeler is already running)', but StartFeeler unconditionally does `go p.feelerLoop(...)`. There is no running-flag/sync.Once guard (confirmed by grep). A caller trusting the comment and calling it twice (e.g. on a config reload) leaks goroutines, each firing periodic Query fan-outs, multiplying outbound query load per tick.
confirmed.suggestion: Add an atomic bool / sync.Once guard so repeated StartSync calls are genuine no-ops, or fix the comment to state that the caller must ensure single invocation.

confirmed.title: Three misbehavior score constants are defined but never charged
confirmed.description: ScoreMalformedResult, ScoreStaleTxID, and ScoreInsufficientPoW are documented as the charges for semantically-garbage results, stale/replayed txids, and under-PoW records, but grep shows none of them are referenced outside their definitions. In particular routeResult/routeReject drop unmatched-txid messages silently with no score (the documented replay-detection signal is dead), and ingestSyncRecords never charges ScoreInsufficientPoW despite the comment promising PoW enforcement. The anti-abuse posture is weaker than the code comments imply.
confirmed.suggestion: Either wire these charges into routeResult (stale txid), a semantic Result validator (malformed result), and the record-ingest PoW check, or remove the constants and their comments so the implemented policy matches the documented one.

confirmed.title: PeerAnnounce is sent fire-and-forget from inside the read loop with no error path
confirmed.description: OnRemoteHandshake spawns `go func(){ _ = sender.Send(addr, payload) }()` per capable handshake. The send error is discarded and the goroutine is unbounded by anything other than handshake rate. If sender.Send blocks (engine write path under backpressure), these goroutines accumulate one per handshake. Low risk in practice but unbounded and silent.
confirmed.suggestion: Bound this with the engine's normal write path or at least log Send failures at Debug; consider a small worker rather than a goroutine-per-handshake.

confirmed.title: mergeResponses double-counts a peer that repeats an infohash in one Result
confirmed.description: merge sums h.Rank and appends ir.peer to Sources for every Hit in a peer's Result. A malicious or buggy responder that lists the same infohash multiple times in one Result inflates that hit's Score (toward the 1000 cap) and lists the same peer address multiple times in Sources, skewing ranking and the source-diversity signal.
confirmed.suggestion: Track which infohashes a given peer has already contributed within one Result and skip duplicates (or dedup Sources).

confirmed.title: Publish marked successful even when getput.Put reaches zero DHT nodes, then rate-limiter suppresses retry
confirmed.description: anacrolix getput.Put (vendored exts/getput/getput.go:155-172) ranges over op.Closest() and returns a nil error even when the closest-node set is empty or every per-node s.Put failed (per-node errors are only logged inside the library). publishOne treats nil as success and calls MarkPublished(keyword, time.Now()). Because publishOne then skips any keyword whose LastPublished is newer than MinPutInterval (default 55m), a put that actually reached zero nodes (fresh node with an empty/cold routing table, transient network partition, or all-peers-rejected) marks the keyword 'published' and blocks any republish attempt for ~55 minutes. The BEP-44 item never lands, so the keyword is undiscoverable for that window despite the manifest reporting healthy PublishCount. This is a fail-open on the publish/finalization step.
confirmed.suggestion: Treat zero-node puts as failure: have getput return (or expose via stats) the number of nodes successfully written and require >=1 before MarkPublished; or wrap the put with op stats (getput.Put returns *traversal.Stats) and call MarkFailed when no node accepted the value. At minimum, do not advance LastPublished (which gates the rate-limiter) unless at least one node confirmed the put.

confirmed.title: Eviction size estimate uses ts=0 while the live encoder injects a 10-digit timestamp, so near-cap entries can fail to publish
confirmed.description: AddHit's eviction loop stops when EstimateValueSize(KeywordValue{Hits: entry.Hits}) <= MaxValueBytes. EstimateValueSize marshals with Ts==0, which bencodes as '2:tsi0e' (7 bytes). At publish time, EncodeValue (schema.go:78) overwrites Ts with time.Now().Unix(), a 10-digit value bencoded as '2:tsi1700000000e' (~16 bytes), i.e. ~9 bytes larger. An entry that the manifest believes fits exactly at MaxValueBytes (1000) therefore encodes to >1000 at put time, EncodeValue returns 'exceeds BEP-44 cap', publishOne calls MarkFailed, and that keyword can never publish until enough hits are removed by other means. The manifest_test eviction case only asserts EstimateValueSize <= cap, never that EncodeValue (with a live Ts) also stays under, so the gap is untested.
confirmed.suggestion: Account for the live timestamp width in the estimate: have EstimateValueSize set Ts to a representative non-zero value (e.g. time.Now().Unix()) before marshaling, or reserve a fixed headroom (e.g. evict until estimate <= MaxValueBytes-16). Add a test that runs the full AddHit-then-EncodeValue path on a near-cap entry.

confirmed.title: DecodeValue/DecodePPMI parse untrusted DHT bytes with no input-size bound
confirmed.description: The read path (AnacrolixGetter.Get -> DecodeValue, GetPPMI -> DecodePPMI) bencode-unmarshals res.V from a remote node with no length check. BEP-44-conforming storage caps v at 1000 bytes, but a non-conforming or malicious node can return up to the UDP datagram limit (~64KB), from which DecodeValue will allocate a Hits slice. Impact is bounded by UDP size so it is not catastrophic, but the encode side enforces MaxValueBytes while the decode side does not, which is an asymmetric, defense-in-depth gap on the only place this package ingests untrusted bytes.
confirmed.suggestion: Reject payloads longer than MaxValueBytes (and MaxPPMIValueBytes) at the top of DecodeValue/DecodePPMI before unmarshaling, mirroring the encode-side cap.

confirmed.title: Sharding schema is defined but neither written nor read; oversize entries silently drop oldest hits
confirmed.description: KeywordValue.More and SaltForShard() document a multi-shard scheme ('Searchers fetch shard 0 first, then fan out'), but the publisher never sets More or writes shard 1+ (AddHit instead evicts the oldest hit, manifest.go:156-158), and Lookup.legacyQuery only ever queries shard 0 (the bare keyword salt) and ignores the More field. The result is silent data loss for popular keywords (oldest hits vanish) plus dead API surface that implies a capability the code does not have, which will mislead future maintainers and any external implementer reading this as a spec.
confirmed.suggestion: Either implement shard spill+read (publisher writes shard N and sets More; lookup follows More to fetch additional shards) or remove SaltForShard/More and document the eviction-based cap as the intended behavior so the on-wire schema and code agree.

confirmed.title: B-tree reader crashes on cyclic/self-referential interior pages (stack overflow DoS)
confirmed.description: walkToLeaves recurses with r.walkToLeaves(int(ch.ChildIndex), ...) on ChildIndex values read straight out of an interior page, with no visited-set, no depth bound, and no requirement that a child piece index be greater than the current one. The interior page structure is NOT covered by any signature: the trailer signs only TreeFingerprint, which BuildBTree computes over the canonical leaf-record stream, so interior ChildIndex bytes are unauthenticated. A malicious publisher publishes a valid BEP-46 pointer to a tree whose root (piece 0) has a single child with ChildIndex=0 (pointing at itself). OpenBTree succeeds (trailer sig + NumPages check pass), then any Find() call recurses infinitely and dies with 'fatal error: stack overflow' — an uncatchable crash of the whole process. This is reachable from cmd/swartznet/cmd_aggregate.go and the daemon aggregate path on trees fetched from arbitrary publishers. I reproduced it: a one-page self-referential root reliably triggers 'goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit / fatal error: stack overflow'.
confirmed.suggestion: In walkToLeaves enforce a strict invariant that children point downward and within range: reject any ch.ChildIndex <= pieceIdx (root is piece 0, children must be > 0 and strictly increasing per BFS layout) and >= NumPieces, returning an error rather than recursing. Additionally pass and decrement a depth budget (e.g. bounded by NumPieces or a small constant like 64) and fail closed when exhausted. A visited-set keyed by piece index also works. Add a regression test feeding a self-referential and a back-pointing interior page.

confirmed.title: Find can blow up combinatorially on a DAG-shaped (non-cyclic) tree
confirmed.description: Even short of an outright cycle, walkToLeaves never deduplicates visited pieces. A malicious tree where many interior pages all list the same set of lower-level children (a DAG, not a tree) causes the same subtrees to be re-walked exponentially. With ~N interior pages each pointing at the same K children, work is multiplicative rather than the intended O(log N) + matching-leaves. This is CPU/allocation exhaustion from a single small fetched file, again unauthenticated because interior structure isn't signed. The monotonic-downward ChildIndex check proposed for the cycle fix largely prevents this too, but it should be called out as a distinct goal.
confirmed.suggestion: Require strictly increasing, downward, in-range child indices (top-down BFS layout already guarantees this for honest builders), and/or track a visited set so each piece is decoded at most once per query. Cap total leaves collected as a defensive secondary bound.

confirmed.title: VerifyFingerprint trusts attacker-controlled NumRecords/page kinds before the count check
confirmed.description: VerifyFingerprint iterates every piece, decoding leaves and hashing records, and only compares count against trailer.NumRecords at the end. A crafted file with a huge NumPieces (consistent trailer NumPages) forces a full scan and unbounded record accumulation in the hash loop before any mismatch is detected. Less severe than walkToLeaves since it is linear in file size (which is already bounded by the downloaded torrent), but it does decode/verify-allocate for every leaf with no early budget.
confirmed.suggestion: Bail out early once count exceeds trailer.NumRecords, and consider capping NumPages/NumRecords against a sane ceiling derived from file size in OpenBTree so downstream scans are pre-bounded.

confirmed.title: recordFailure sets lastRefresh, conflating failures with successful publishes for throttling
confirmed.description: recordFailure sets p.lastRefresh = time.Now() on every failure (including the common 'empty local index' case that fires on the very first tick of a fresh node). RefreshNow throttles on lastRefresh, so a user pressing a manual-refresh button right after an empty-index failure gets ErrTooSoon even though nothing was actually published. It also makes Status().LastRefresh report a time at which no pointer was published, which is misleading for the 'is my pointer still alive (<2h)' question the field exists to answer.
confirmed.suggestion: Track failure time separately from successful-publish time (e.g. lastAttempt vs lastRefresh), throttle RefreshNow on lastAttempt, and let Status expose the last successful publish time so keepalive/expiry reasoning stays correct.

confirmed.title: Unfollow during a sync pass re-inserts a stale lastSync entry
confirmed.description: runOnce snapshots the follow list, then for each pub does the (slow) Sync and writes w.lastSync[pub] = res under lock. If Unfollow(pub) runs after the snapshot but before the write-back, Unfollow deletes lastSync[pub], but runOnce then re-creates it, leaving a result for a publisher no longer followed. AllResults/LastSync will surface it indefinitely (it is only ever cleaned by a subsequent Unfollow). A small, persistent state-leak, not a crash.
confirmed.suggestion: Before writing back, re-check membership under the lock: if _, ok := w.follows[pub]; ok { w.lastSync[pub] = res }. Otherwise drop the result.

confirmed.title: Dead no-op block in EncodeInterior first-child separator handling
confirmed.description: The `if i == 0 && len(c.Separator) != 0 { ... }` block contains only a comment and does nothing — the separator is written verbatim regardless. It reads as if it intends to zero out the first child's separator (which the reader/spec treat as implicitly empty / -infinity) but does not, so an honest builder that passes a non-empty first separator silently produces a page whose first child carries a real lower bound. Harmless today because packInteriorLevel always passes nil for the first child, but it is a latent trap.
confirmed.suggestion: Either drop the dead block entirely, or make it enforce the invariant by forcing the first child's separator to empty before writing it, so the encoder is robust to callers that don't pre-clear it.

confirmed.title: No CSRF/Origin protection on state-mutating localhost endpoints
confirmed.description: The API binds loopback and has zero CSRF defense (no Origin/Referer/Host allowlist, no custom-header requirement, no token). The pause/resume/remove handlers (controlOne) read only r.PathValue and require no request body or content-type, so they are triggerable as CORS 'simple requests'. Any web page the user visits while the daemon runs can run fetch('http://localhost:7654/torrents/<ih>/pause',{method:'POST',mode:'no-cors'}) — POST is a CORS-simple method, so no preflight blocks it — and likewise resume/remove torrents, change rate-limit/queue (POST /config/*), and (if the attacker guesses or learns an infohash) flag it to corrupt reputation or confirm it into the known-good Bloom filter. The browser sends these cross-origin without the user's knowledge. A DNS-rebinding attack additionally defeats any naive same-origin assumption. This is a real, exploitable CSRF surface on every endpoint that changes state.
confirmed.suggestion: Add middleware that, for all non-GET (and ideally GET state probes too) requests, rejects when the Origin/Referer header is present and not http://localhost:PORT / http://127.0.0.1:PORT, AND validates the Host header against a loopback allowlist to stop DNS rebinding. Alternatively require a non-simple header (e.g. X-SwartzNet: 1) on all mutating endpoints so the browser must preflight, and reject requests lacking it. Apply in withMaxBodyBytes' wrapper or a new middleware in server.go Start().

confirmed.title: Operator can bind unauthenticated API to non-loopback with no warning
confirmed.description: Start() calls net.Listen('tcp', s.addr) with whatever --api-addr the operator passed (e.g. 0.0.0.0:7654). The API has no authentication of any kind. Combined with the lack of a Host/Origin check, binding to a routable interface exposes torrent control, follow-list mutation, capability changes, rate-limit control, and reputation/Bloom mutation to the entire LAN/internet. The default is localhost, but nothing fails closed or even warns when a non-loopback address is configured.
confirmed.suggestion: When the resolved listen host is not a loopback address, either refuse to start without an explicit opt-in flag, or log a prominent WARN that the API is unauthenticated and reachable off-host. Pair this with the Host/Origin allowlist above so even an off-host bind still requires a matching Host.

confirmed.title: Publisher pubkey is never populated in /status
confirmed.description: PublisherStatus has a PubKey field and the web UI reads s.publisher.pubkey to render a 'pubkey' row (app.js:504-506), but handleStatus sets only TotalKeywords/TotalHits/Keywords and never out.Publisher.PubKey. The pubkey row therefore never appears, and any programmatic client of /status always sees an empty publisher pubkey even when a publisher is active.
confirmed.suggestion: Populate out.Publisher.PubKey from the publisher's identity (e.g. s.publisher.Status() or a PubKeyHex accessor) when s.publisher != nil.

confirmed.title: Client-supplied search timeouts are unbounded
confirmed.description: SwarmTimeoutMs and DHTTimeoutMs are taken directly from the request with only a zero->default substitution; there is no upper clamp. A local client can pass e.g. swarm_timeout_ms=999999999, holding a swarm/DHT query (and the handler goroutine) open far longer than intended. WriteTimeout (30s) does not cancel the handler, only failing the eventual write; the context lives for timeout+500ms or until the client disconnects. Low impact since the API is loopback, but it is an easy resource-exhaustion lever.
confirmed.suggestion: Clamp both timeouts to a sane ceiling (e.g. min(req.SwarmTimeoutMs, 30s)) mirroring how maxSearchLimit clamps Limit.

confirmed.title: Companion publisher writes to DataDir, ignoring configured CompanionDir
confirmed.description: The companion publisher/subscriber are gated on opts.Cfg.CompanionDir != "", but the publisher's output directory is set with cpOpts.Dir = opts.Cfg.DataDir. CompanionDir is therefore used only as an enable flag and never as the actual storage location. config.Default() sets CompanionDir to ~/.local/share/swartznet/companion (distinct from DataDir ~/.local/share/swartznet/data, per the field doc), so in the default install the gzipped JSON content index and wrapping .torrent are written into the downloaded-content directory instead of the companion directory the user configured. An operator who sets CompanionDir to a separate disk/path sees their setting silently ignored, and companion artifacts pollute the content tree (and can collide with torrent file paths).
confirmed.suggestion: Set cpOpts.Dir = opts.Cfg.CompanionDir (the value already gating the block). If DataDir was intended for a reason, document it and rename the gate accordingly; otherwise this is a straight one-line fix. Add a daemon test that sets CompanionDir != DataDir and asserts companion files land under CompanionDir.

confirmed.title: HTTPS anchor-bootstrap fetch does not enforce https scheme
confirmed.description: FallbackToHTTPS / httpGetClient.Get accept any URL scheme; neither rejects http://. The fetched anchors are EigenTrust-style trust seeds admitted to the Lookup set and (for anchors) seeded into the reputation tracker with a high score. The file's own comment calls this 'the one HTTPS dependency' and bases its threat model on TLS integrity, but a plaintext URL (operator typo, downgraded config, or a release that ships an http DefaultBootstrapURL) lets an on-path attacker inject attacker-controlled anchor pubkeys, poisoning the trust set. DefaultBootstrapURL is empty in dev, but the function is exported and reachable with caller-supplied URLs.
confirmed.suggestion: Parse the URL and return an error unless scheme == "https" (allow an explicit test-only override, e.g. a localhost exemption guarded behind a flag). Enforce in both FallbackToHTTPS and httpGetClient.Get.

confirmed.title: AnchorReputation / CandidateReputation options are dead config
confirmed.description: BootstrapOptions.AnchorReputation and CandidateReputation are documented, validated, and defaulted, but never applied. admit() calls tracker.MarkSeeded(pub, label) which takes no score, and candidate sources call no scoring at all. An operator who sets AnchorReputation=0.9 (or any value) gets no behavioral change, contradicting the field docs ('the natural interpretation of opts.AnchorReputation'). This is a silent no-op that misleads tuning.
confirmed.suggestion: Either thread the score through to the tracker (extend MarkSeeded or add a seed-with-score path) or remove the two fields and their defaulting logic and adjust the doc comments to reflect that anchors get the tracker's fixed seeded bonus.

confirmed.title: Anchor-fetch goroutine in New is not awaited or cancel-tracked on Close
confirmed.description: New spawns a background goroutine running boot.RunAnchors(ctx) when anchors are present. Close has no handle to it and does not wait for or cancel it; it relies entirely on the caller cancelling the ctx passed to New. If a caller calls Close() but keeps the ctx alive (a reasonable assumption given Close takes no ctx), the goroutine keeps fan-out GetPPMI calls running against a DHT that engine.Close is concurrently tearing down. With the empty dev anchor set the guard skips the goroutine, so this only bites production anchored builds.
confirmed.suggestion: Store a cancel func (derive a child context in New) and call it at the top of Close, optionally with a WaitGroup to join the anchor goroutine, so Close deterministically stops bootstrap work before tearing down the engine.

confirmed.title: Explicit --key / --identity path silently mints a new identity instead of failing closed
confirmed.description: loadPrivKey's explicit-path branch is commented "Explicit path: load only, don't auto-generate" but calls identity.LoadOrCreate(keyPath), which creates a brand-new ed25519 keypair at that path if the file is absent. Failure scenario: an operator runs `swartznet aggregate build --key /mnt/usb/pub.key ...` after the USB key failed to mount (or with a typo). Instead of erroring, the CLI generates a fresh unknown key, signs every Aggregate record with it, and writes a published index that no downloader will ever trust — silently severing publisher reputation. The same issue applies to `create --identity <path>` in cmd_create.go:86, which also uses LoadOrCreate. This violates the 'identity is never regenerated implicitly' invariant for user-specified paths.
confirmed.suggestion: Add a load-only path: stat the file first and return an error if it does not exist when an explicit --key/--identity was given (only the empty-path default should auto-create). Either export identity.loadFromDisk or add an identity.Load(path) that returns os.ErrNotExist unwrapped, and use it in the explicit-path branches.

confirmed.title: aggregate-build default identity path ignores XDG_DATA_HOME, diverging from the daemon
confirmed.description: defaultIdentityPath() hardcodes home + "/.local/share/swartznet/identity.key", but internal/config resolves the identity path via swartznetShareRoot() which honors $XDG_DATA_HOME (config.go:407). Failure scenario: a user (or container) with XDG_DATA_HOME=/data set runs the daemon, which creates/uses /data/swartznet/identity.key, then runs `swartznet aggregate build` with no --key; this CLI instead reads ~/.local/share/swartznet/identity.key, finds it missing, and (per the prior finding) LoadOrCreate mints a *second* identity. The build is signed by a different pubkey than everything the daemon publishes, so the records are orphaned. The in-file comment claims it 'mirrors the XDG path the daemon uses' — it does not.
confirmed.suggestion: Drop the local defaultIdentityPath and use config.Default().IdentityPath (as cmd_create.go already does at line 84) so the default resolution is identical to the daemon's, including XDG_DATA_HOME.

confirmed.title: create --seed returns exit 0 on SIGINT instead of 130
confirmed.description: The --seed branch blocks on <-ctx.Done() and then falls through to `return exitOK`, so a Ctrl-C during seeding exits 0. Every other long-running path (cmdAdd) maps signal cancellation to exitInterrupt (130) via reportRunErr(ctx.Err()). Scripts that distinguish clean-exit from interrupt by exit code will misclassify a seeded create that was interrupted.
confirmed.suggestion: After <-ctx.Done(), `return reportRunErr(ctx.Err(), stderr)` to stay consistent with cmdAdd's interrupt handling.

confirmed.title: Infohash validation checks length but not hex-ness
confirmed.description: flag/confirm/index/files all validate `len(infoHash) != 40` but never confirm the characters are hex. A 40-char non-hex argument (e.g. a typo'd word of the right length) is accepted by the CLI and forwarded to the daemon, which then rejects it with a less obvious API-status error. Same pattern in cmd_index.go:32, cmd_files.go:49 and :102. Low impact because the server fails closed, but the user gets a worse error message than necessary.
confirmed.suggestion: After the length check, validate with hex.DecodeString (or a regexp) and emit 'infohash must be 40 hex characters' locally before the round-trip.

confirmed.title: Dangerous testing flags (--regtest, --dht-insecure) ship unhidden in the production CLI
confirmed.description: --dht-insecure disables BEP-42 node-ID security and --regtest enables accelerated publisher/companion timings; both are documented 'TESTING ONLY — never run against mainnet'. They are real flags on the production `add` command with no guard beyond the help string. A user copy-pasting a testbed command against mainline DHT would weaken their node-ID security on the public network. Not a wire-compat break (BEP-42 non-enforcement is still interoperable) but it lowers the node's Sybil resistance on the real network.
confirmed.suggestion: Gate these behind an env var (e.g. SWARTZNET_UNSAFE=1) or a build tag so they are inert in release binaries, or at minimum print a loud stderr warning when either is set against a non-loopback DHT.

confirmed.title: Follow list rows are ordered non-deterministically, so Unfollow targets the wrong publisher
confirmed.description: refresh() builds the follow rows by ranging over the map returned by CompSub.Following() (subscriber.go:381 returns map[[32]byte]string). Go map iteration order is randomized per range, so ct.follows is reshuffled on every 4s poll. Two concrete failures: (1) the right-click context menu uses ct.followSelected (an index set by OnSelected at line 133-134); after the next refresh that index now points to a different publisher, so 'Unfollow' / 'Copy public key' acts on the wrong publisher; (2) rows visibly jump around every poll. Because Unfollow is destructive, this can silently unfollow a publisher the user did not intend to.
confirmed.suggestion: Sort the rows slice deterministically (e.g. by label then pubkey, or by pubkey) before assigning ct.follows in refresh(), so a given screen position maps stably to a given publisher across refreshes. Prefer keying selection by pubkey rather than by row index for the menu path.

confirmed.title: filesDialog priority Select re-fires OnChanged on every refresh, issuing spurious SetFilePriority writes
confirmed.description: In the List UpdateCell, prioSelect.SetSelected(f.Priority) is called at line 95 while the recycled widget's OnChanged handler from its previous binding is still attached, and the real handler is only reassigned at line 98. Fyne's Select.SetSelected -> updateSelected (select.go:200-331 in fyne v2.7.3) unconditionally invokes OnChanged whenever the text matches an option, even if the value is unchanged. So on each 2s tick (and on every scroll/re-sort), the stale closure fires SetFilePriority with the PREVIOUS row's captured idx but the NEW row's priority value — writing the wrong file's priority when the list is re-sorted or scrolled, and at minimum spamming redundant engine writes for every visible file every 2 seconds.
confirmed.suggestion: Set prioSelect.OnChanged = nil before calling SetSelected, then assign the real handler afterward; or compare and skip. e.g. `prioSelect.OnChanged = nil; prioSelect.SetSelected(f.Priority); prioSelect.OnChanged = func(...) {...}`.

confirmed.title: Already-seeding torrents fire a false 'Download complete' notification on startup
confirmed.description: notificationLoop starts with an empty lastNotified map, so on the first 3s tick every torrent already in 'seeding' state (content downloaded in a prior session, a freshly-created torrent seeded immediately, or a .torrent added for already-complete content) emits a 'Download complete' OS notification even though nothing was downloaded this session.
confirmed.suggestion: On the first poll, seed lastNotified with all currently-seeding infohashes without notifying (prime the map before the loop, or skip notifications until a torrent is observed transitioning out of seeding into seeding).

confirmed.title: SelectTab comment claims case-insensitive but only matches two exact spellings
confirmed.description: The doc comment says 'Case-insensitive' but the switch only matches exact lowercase and Title-case forms; '--tab DOWNLOADS' or a trailing space silently no-ops. Low impact (flag help documents lowercase), but the comment is misleading.
confirmed.suggestion: Either lowercase+TrimSpace the input before the switch, or correct the comment to state the accepted spellings.

confirmed.title: Seed-list pubkey stored without lowercasing, so seed bonus never applies for uppercase hex
confirmed.description: LoadSeedList validates e.PubKey decodes to 32 bytes but then calls MarkSeeded(PubKeyHex(e.PubKey), ...) with the raw, un-normalized string. The canonical key form used everywhere else is lowercase hex: reputation.PubKey() uses hex.EncodeToString (lowercase), and every caller in dhtindex/lookup.go derives keys via reputation.PubKey(info.PubKey). If a curated seed-list JSON contains uppercase or mixed-case hex (a perfectly valid hex encoding), the record is stored under an uppercase key while IsSeeded/AnySeeded/Score lookups query the lowercase key. Result: the seed bonus and heavy-tail float-rule silently never fire for that publisher, defeating the cold-start bootstrapping the seed list exists to provide. This is also a silent reputation-correctness divergence with no error surfaced.
confirmed.suggestion: Normalize before storing: t.MarkSeeded(PubKeyHex(strings.ToLower(e.PubKey)), e.Label). Alternatively reconstruct from the decoded bytes via reputation.PubKey on the [32]byte to guarantee canonical form. Add a test with an uppercase seed entry asserting IsSeeded(lowercase) is true.

confirmed.title: Corrupt Bloom file with m=0 causes divide-by-zero panic on Test/Add
confirmed.description: readBloom reads m from the file header but never enforces m >= 1 (or k >= 1). NewBloomFilter clamps m to at least 1 via optimalSize, but a file loaded from disk bypasses that. The only consistency check is `bitsLen > (m+63)/64+1`; with m=0 that bound is 1, so a crafted/truncated-then-padded header with m=0 and bitsLen<=1 passes validation. The resulting BloomFilter has m=0, and the first Test or Add call reaches indices(), which computes `(h1 + i*h2) % b.m` => integer divide by zero => panic that crashes the daemon. known-good.bloom is a local file, but partial-write/disk-corruption (e.g. crash mid-Save before the atomic rename window, or manual tampering) can produce this and turn a confirm/auto-confirm event into a hard crash rather than a recoverable load error.
confirmed.suggestion: In readBloom, reject m==0 and k==0 with an error (e.g. `if m == 0 || k == 0 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("reputation: invalid bloom params m=%d k=%d", m, k) }`). Optionally validate bitsLen == (m+63)/64 exactly. Add a bloom_errors_test case feeding a header with m=0 and asserting an error, not a panic.

confirmed.title: Loaded private key public half is trusted without verifying it matches the seed
confirmed.description: loadFromDisk constructs ed25519.PrivateKey(raw) from 64 bytes and derives PublicKey from priv.Public(), which simply returns bytes [32:64] of the file rather than re-deriving the public key from the 32-byte seed [0:32]. If the file's trailing 32 bytes are corrupted independently of the seed, Identity.PublicKey will not correspond to the actual signing seed, so every signature produced will fail verification against the advertised pubkey, with no error at load time. This is a local-corruption-only scenario, but it would manifest as confusing 'signature does not verify' failures far from the root cause.
confirmed.suggestion: Re-derive and compare: pub := ed25519.NewKeyFromSeed(raw[:32]).Public().(ed25519.PublicKey); if !bytes.Equal(pub, raw[32:]) return an error ('corrupt key file: public half does not match seed'). This makes corruption fail loud at load.

confirmed.title: Bloom double-hashing can collapse to a single bit when second hash is 0 mod m
confirmed.description: indices() uses double hashing out[i] = (h1 + i*h2) % m without forcing h2 to be nonzero/odd. For any input where h2 % m == 0, all k indices collapse to h1 % m, so that item effectively sets/tests a single bit. This raises the practical false-positive rate for those inputs above the configured target. With 20-byte SHA-1 inputs and a ~9.6M-bit filter the probability is tiny, but the standard mitigation is cheap. False positives only over-rank a non-known-good hit (the comment acknowledges this is harmless), so severity is low.
confirmed.suggestion: Force a nonzero, coprime-ish step, e.g. h2 |= 1 (make it odd) before the loop, which is the conventional Kirsch-Mitzenmacher fix and guarantees k distinct strides.

confirmed.title: Node.IndexDir reports a path that does not hold the node's actual Bleve index
confirmed.description: spawnNode sets cfg.IndexDir = root/"bleve" but then opens the real index at root/"bleve-idx" via indexer.Open and attaches it with eng.SetIndex. engine.New never opens cfg.IndexDir (SetIndex is the only index path), so cfg.IndexDir is dead config, yet the returned Node records IndexDir: cfg.IndexDir (root/bleve). Any future scenario test that trusts Node.IndexDir to locate index files on disk would look in the wrong, empty directory. Today no test reads Node.IndexDir so there is no active bug, but it is a trap waiting for the first test that does.
confirmed.suggestion: Either set cfg.IndexDir to the same directory passed to indexer.Open (drop the separate bleve-idx dir and reuse root/bleve), or set Node.IndexDir = bleveDir so the reported path matches where the index actually lives.

confirmed.title: Config.Validate does not reject Regtest/DHTInsecure, relying solely on an engine-side Warn
confirmed.description: Validate() checks DataDir and ListenPort but performs no sanity check that the production-dangerous flags (Regtest hammers the mainline DHT every ~5s; DHTInsecure disables BEP-42 Sybil resistance) are not set in a non-test build. The only safety net is engine.New logging engine.regtest_mode_active at Warn (confirmed at engine.go:741), which an operator can easily miss in logs. This is defense-in-depth, not a defect: the flags are intentional knobs and the docstrings are emphatic, but a misconfigured config.json could silently put a real node into regtest/insecure mode.
confirmed.suggestion: Consider a build-tagged or env-gated guard (e.g. require an explicit SWARTZNET_ALLOW_REGTEST=1 to set Regtest outside tests) so the dangerous flags fail closed rather than only warning. Low priority given current CLI never sets them.

rejected.title: FetchCompanionTorrent returns a path built from attacker-controlled info.Name
rejected.reason:
The core security claim — that a crafted `info.Name` with path traversal causes `decodeFile` to open an attacker-chosen path — is not reachable.

Line 1253 (`return filepath.Join(e.cfg.DataDir, info.Name), nil`) is only reached after `h.T.GotInfo()` fires (line 1211). `GotInfo` only fires when `onSetInfo()` is called, which in turn only happens when `setInfo()` returns without error (torrent.go lines 674-678, 686-690). `setInfo()` calls `OpenTorrent()` (torrent.go line 560), which does an `isSubFilepath(dir, filePath)` check (file-client.go lines 92-95). A traversal `info.Name` like `../../etc/passwd` produces `filePath = "/etc/passwd"`, which fails `isSubFilepath`, causing `OpenTorrent` to return an error, `setInfo` to return an error, and `onSetInfo` — and therefore `close(t.gotMetainfoC)` — to never execute. So `GotInfo()` never fires; `FetchCompanionTorrent` blocks until context timeout and returns `("", ctx.Err())`, not the bad path.

There is a narrow divergence if `info.NameUtf8` and `info.Name` differ (anacrolix uses `BestName()` which prefers `NameUtf8`, while line 1253 uses `info.Name`). This is a real but benign bug: the subscriber gets a decode error on wrong-file open, not a path-confusion security issue. It is not remotely exploitable for arbitrary reads since the path must still be a sub-path of `DataDir`.

The single-file enforcement at lines 1217-1218 already rejects multi-file torrents, further narrowing attack surface. The finding overstates both the severity and reachability of the claimed failure scenario; the anacrolix `isSubFilepath` guard is precisely the mitigation described in the suggested fix.
